title: Excuse me, where is...?
goal: Ask for directions, understand them, and use the imperative for the first time.
bekal: politely ask a stranger where a place is
form commands from verbs you already know

dialogs.title: حِوَار — فِي الشَّارِعِ
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost, looking for the post office in the city center.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Excuse me, where is the post office?

lines.speaker: رَجُل:
lines.id: It's close. Walk straight on to the traffic lights.

lines.speaker: رَجُل:
lines.text: ثُمَّ اِنْعَطِفْ يَمِينًا. اَلْمَكْتَبُ عَلَى يَسَارِكَ.
lines.id: Then turn right. The post office is on your left.
lines.literal: then turn to-right. the-office on left-your.

lines.speaker: رَجُل:
lines.id: Yes, between the bank and the mosque.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: شُكْرًا جَزِيلًا! أَنَا لَسْتُ مِنْ هُنَا.
lines.baca: shukran jaziilan! anaa lastu min hunaa.
lines.id: Thank you so much! I'm not from here.
lines.literal: thanks abundant! I am-not from here.

lines.speaker: رَجُل:
lines.id: You're welcome. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: From Indonesia. I'm here to study.

lines.speaker: رَجُل:
lines.text: أَهْلًا بِكَ فِي مِصْرَ! حَظًّا سَعِيدًا.
lines.baca: ahlan bika fii Miṣr! haẓẓan sa'iidan.
lines.literal: welcome with-you in Egypt! luck happy.

notes: **لَوْ سَمَحْتَ is the safest opener.** Literally "if you permit". To a woman: لَوْ سَمَحْتِ. Firing a question at a stranger with no opener at all sounds pushy, just as it does in English.
**اِمْشِ, اِنْعَطِفْ — the imperative.** They all start with اِ and are built from the present-tense verb with its prefix dropped. See the grammar box; the pattern is more regular than it looks.

**يَمِينًا and يَسَارًا — tanwin fathah again.** The ending ـًا turns a noun into an adverb: يَمِين (right) → يَمِينًا (to the right), مَشْي (walking) → مَشْيًا (on foot). You have already met the same pattern in شُكْرًا and غَدًا.

**عَلَى يَسَارِكَ — "on your left".** Right and left are always relative to the person, as in English. Compass points are for longer distances: شَمَال (north), جَنُوب (south), شَرْق (east), غَرْب (west).
**لَسْتُ = لَيْسَ for "I".** لَيْسَ changes with its subject like a past-tense verb: لَسْتُ (I am not), لَسْتَ (you are not), لَيْسَ (he is not), لَيْسَتْ (she is not), لَسْنَا (we are not).

**لِلدِّرَاسَةِ = لِ + الدِّرَاسَة.** The alif of اَلْ drops out after لِ, and the sounds merge: *lid-diraasah*. Same thing in لِلْبَيْتِ (for the house), بِالسَّيَّارَةِ (by car), and فِي الْبَيْتِ, read *fil-bait*.
**حَتَّى means "until".** حَتَّى الْإِشَارَةِ (up to the traffic lights), حَتَّى الْآنَ (until now), مِنْ ... حَتَّى ... (from ... until ...). It can also mean "even" — context tells them apart.
**حَظًّا سَعِيدًا** is "good luck". Other short well-wishing phrases you will hear often: بِالتَّوْفِيقِ (all the best), رِحْلَةً سَعِيدَةً (have a good trip), بِالشِّفَاءِ (get well soon).

grammars.title: Fi'il amr — the imperative
body: How it works: take the present-tense verb for "you", drop the prefix تَـ, and put a sukun on the last letter. If what remains starts with a consonant without a vowel, add اِ in front.
after: The vowel on the initial اِ follows the verb's middle vowel: if the middle is ḍammah, it becomes اُ (اُكْتُبْ); otherwise اِ (اِذْهَبْ, اِجْلِسْ).
**You don't forbid by changing the command form**, but with لَا + the present-tense verb: لَا تَذْهَبْ (don't go), لَا تَنْسَ (don't forget), لَا تَقْلَقْ (don't worry).

grammars.title: Directions

head: Arabic
Pronunciation
Meaning
rows: at the end of the street

after: If the directions come too fast: مَرَّةً أُخْرَى، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ ("once more, please") or بِبُطْءٍ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ ("slowly, please"). These two sentences are far more useful than ten extra vocabulary words.

blocks.text: Notice again the prefix مَ- that marks a place: مَكْتَب, مَحَطَّة, مَطَار, مَتْحَف, مَدْرَسَة, مَسْجِد. Six words with the same pattern at once — and English has already borrowed two of them as *madrasa* and, via Spanish and French, *mosque*.

blocks.title: Who to ask
items: In Arab cities people are almost always happy to help a lost foreigner — often to the point of walking you there. What you should know: some people would rather guess than admit they don't know, because admitting it feels like refusing to help.
So a safe habit: ask two people at two different spots. If the answers match, keep going. If they differ, ask a third.

blocks.text: أَنَا تَائِهٌ ("I'm lost") is one of the most useful sentences in this book, and it almost always brings help right away. A woman says أَنَا تَائِهَةٌ.

exercises.prompt: Make these into commands (to a man, then to a woman).

items: Excuse me, where is the bank?
Walk straight on to the traffic lights.
The pharmacy is opposite the mosque.
How far is it from here?

exercises.prompt: Give directions from your home to each place below, two sentences each.

answers: اُكْتُبْ / اُكْتُبِي — اِجْلِسْ / اِجْلِسِي — اِذْهَبْ / اِذْهَبِي — اِسْمَعْ / اِسْمَعِي — خُذْ / خُذِي — اُنْظُرْ / اُنْظُرِي
لَوْ سَمَحْتَ، أَيْنَ الْبَنْكُ؟ — اِمْشِ مُسْتَقِيمًا حَتَّى الْإِشَارَةِ. — ثُمَّ اِنْعَطِفْ يَسَارًا. — اَلصَّيْدَلِيَّةُ مُقَابِلَ الْمَسْجِدِ. — كَمْ يَبْعُدُ مِنْ هُنَا؟ — أَنَا تَائِهٌ.
لَا تَذْهَبْ إِلَى السُّوقِ. — لَا تَكْتُبْ هُنَا. — لَا تَجْلِسْ عَلَى الْكُرْسِيِّ. — لَا تَأْخُذْ هٰذَا الْكِتَابَ. — لَا تَنْعَطِفْ يَمِينًا.

Example: اُخْرُجْ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ وَاِمْشِ مُسْتَقِيمًا، اَلْمَسْجِدُ عَلَى يَمِينِكَ — اِنْعَطِفْ يَسَارًا عِنْدَ الْإِشَارَةِ، اَلسُّوقُ فِي نِهَايَةِ الشَّارِعِ — اِمْشِ مُسْتَقِيمًا ثُمَّ اُعْبُرِ الشَّارِعَ، اَلْمُسْتَشْفَى مُقَابِلَ الْبَنْكِ — اَلْمَحَطَّةُ قَرِيبَةٌ، بِجَانِبِ الصَّيْدَلِيَّةِ — اِنْعَطِفْ يَمِينًا فِي الزَّاوِيَةِ، اَلْمَدْرَسَةُ أَمَامَكَ
wave: Tomorrow, as you walk out of your house, give yourself directions in Arabic: straight on, turn right, opposite.
